text: {"answer":"Polymorphism in Java means one name or interface can take different behaviors depending on context. It is commonly split into two kinds. Compile-time (static) polymorphism is method overloading, where the compiler picks a method by its parameter list before the program runs [5974f259d0f5#0][5160a72f8912#2]. Runtime (dynamic) polymorphism is method overriding, where the JVM picks the version belonging to the actual object through dynamic method dispatch [5974f259d0f5#0][c5005aa3ff83#0]. Some sources argue the runtime kind is what interviewers usually mean, and that overloading is a naming convenience resolved statically [667aeb21156d#2]. A Medium article contends that true polymorphism exists only through overriding, not overloading [29552994a8fa#0]. This is a minority, opinionated view, since most supporting sources, including GeeksforGeeks, count overloading as a form of polymorphism [5160a72f8912#0]. Overall, the broad definition and the two-type split are well supported, while the dispute concerns whether overloading qualifies.","confidence":80,"one_line":"Polymorphism lets one method name behave differently: compile-time via overloading, runtime via overriding and dynamic dispatch; some argue only overriding counts."}
